rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to test whether the crowded central peaks separate with a shallower slope. The current last peak at 7.16 min leaves room to improve resolution before incurring a time penalty.
The shallower gradient improved the limiting pair substantially, but further lengthening risks a time penalty. Raise temperature by one step to test selectivity while bringing the last peak earlier.

The temperature response suggests the limiting pair is approaching an elution-order reversal. Moving to 55 C tests separation on the other side of that crossover while shortening retention; the other pairs currently have useful resolution margins.

After the apparent order reversal, a slightly steeper gradient may open the limiting pair rather than compress it, as suggested by the earlier slope response. Shortening to 12 minutes tests this while reducing retention and preserving the temperature that gave the best score.

Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Shorten the gradient by one step to test whether full resolution can be retained in a faster run, watching especially the narrowly resolved pairs.

Keep the successful injection 5 slope while trimming the solvent window to remove time spent below the main elution range. This tests a faster method without the slope increase that compromised resolution in injection 6; injection 5 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Injection 5 already secures the maximum score, so test a substantially faster selectivity regime. A steeper gradient and higher temperature may carry the current limiting pair through an order reversal and restore separation on the other side.

Explore the low-temperature selectivity regime, since heating improved one crowded pair but compromised another. Comparing with the existing 10-minute gradients will test whether cooling opens a faster fully resolved alternative; injection 5 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Refine injection 7 with a slightly shallower slope to recover its limiting pair, while trimming the final organic fraction to just above the observed elution window. This targets full resolution with an earlier last peak than injection 5 and keeps the last compound within the gradient.

Slightly reduce the slope from injection 10 to bring its limiting pair above R = 1.5 while preserving the other critical pair’s margin. This tests a second fully resolved method expected to keep the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

With two maximum-score methods secured, test a faster, shifted solvent window at 60 C. Raising the starting organic fraction may strengthen the order reversal seen in injection 8, while the gentler slope should help separate its crowded central cluster.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction and shallower slope can balance the two crowded central gaps in injection 12. Monitor the first pair closely because its resolution may deteriorate as initial retention decreases; the maximum-score methods remain secured.

Test a shallower gradient at 60 C to separate the central cluster in a different selectivity regime. The higher temperature should help keep the last peak near the 10-minute threshold; injection 5 remains the faster maximum-score benchmark.

Trim injection 5’s unused high-organic tail while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope exactly. Its last peak eluted at approximately 0.57 organic fraction, so this method should retain full resolution and the maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test intermediate-temperature selectivity for a faster fully resolved alternative. Cooling slightly from injection 1 may open its limiting central pair without producing the extensive crowding observed at 25 C; the proven maximum-score methods remain the fallback.

Refine around the proven optimum with a slightly shallower slope, aiming to increase the resolution margin of the earlier critical pair while keeping the later pair above 1.5. The last peak should remain well below 10 minutes, preserving maximum CRF if both pairs resolve.

Test a slope between injections 10 and 11 to locate the fastest fully resolved boundary at this starting composition. The limiting pair is predicted to be near R = 1.5, with the last peak slightly earlier than in injection 11.

Test a narrower window with a shallower slope to compensate for the resolution loss caused by raising the starting organic fraction. This explores another fully resolved operating region while keeping initial retention and the expected last peak within acceptable limits.

Test a gradient slope between the fastest fully resolved method and the faster failed injection 6. This should locate the resolution boundary more closely while shortening retention relative to injection 5; the critical earlier pair is the main risk.

Reduce the slope one step from injection 19 to improve its sole unresolved pair, while retaining the later critical pair’s larger margin. This targets a maximum-score alternative with more balanced resolution margins and an expected last peak below 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope one further step from injection 21, targeting full resolution with larger critical-pair margins than the current best methods. The observed retention trend predicts the last peak near 9.3 minutes, still below the time-penalty threshold.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 11 to improve its limiting pair while retaining the later pair’s resolution margin. This targets maximum CRF with better minimum resolution than injection 5 and a shorter run than injection 22.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 22 to shorten retention while retaining its stronger resolution margins. Interpolation between injections 21 and 22 predicts both critical pairs above 1.5 and the last peak near 9 minutes.

Slightly increase the slope from injection 24 to shorten retention while targeting full resolution, based on the boundary bracketed by injections 21 and 24. Injection 5 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method if this final refinement offers no advantage.
